full_article:
The Nepal Automobiles' Association (NASA Nepal) recently organized the Nepal Sim Racing National Championship 2026 at the International Sports Complex in Lalitpur, Nepal. Supported by the FIA Motorsport Funding Program, the project has strengthened grassroots motorsports development in Nepal by providing sim racing training to more than 400 young people.

The championship comprised four regional competitions and one national championship, offering regional exposure to the junior and senior winners, who demonstrated promising talent on the two FIA-accredited sim racing simulators NASA Nepal purchased to support the competition.

The championship used advanced sim racing technology and the iRacing platform, allowing participants to compete on internationally recognized virtual circuits. The event provided an opportunity to develop racing skills, precision, strategic thinking and competitive discipline in a structured digital motorsports environment.

The championship was officially opened by NASA Nepal President Dasarath Risal and Chandra Kumar Rai, chief of the International Sports Complex in Satdobato.

Through the Esport Championship in Nepal project, NASA Nepal aims to expand access to motorsports, identify emerging talent, and create new opportunities for young people to participate in the sport. The initiative supports the continued development of motorsports in Nepal in line with the FIA's commitment to doubling global participation.

In the senior category, Jay Pratap Maskey finished first, followed by Niman Shakya. Maskey recorded a best lap time of approximately 1 minute 22 seconds on the Circuit de Lédenon. In the junior category, Kushal Bhandari secured first place, followed by Sparsha Byanju and Binit Maharjan. Bhushan Kumar Shrestha won the Promotional Challenge category. Winners received cash prizes, medals and certificates.

For more information, read the FIA announcement or visit fia.com.

title: Survey-weighted cross-sectional study links Nepal insurance enrollment with higher curative healthcare use - Bioengineer.org
description: Survey-weighted cross-sectional study links Nepal insurance enrollment with higher curative healthcare use  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
A survey-weighted cross-sectional study in Suryabinayak municipality, Nepal, found that households enrolled in the National Health Insurance Program reported more use of several healthcare services than uninsured households, while preventive service use showed no overall association. The available abstract reports overall utilization of 74.7% among insured households and 53.6% among uninsured households, a statistically significant difference. In adjusted analyses, enrollment was associated with higher odds of overall, outpatient, diagnostic, emergency and inpatient service use, but not preventive services overall.

Researchers conducted a community-based comparative cross-sectional survey from June to July 2025. They randomly selected five of Suryabinayak’s 10 administrative wards, then used two-stage stratified random sampling to recruit 301 households in Bhaktapur: 150 with National Health Insurance Program enrollment and 151 without it. Utilization outcomes covered overall service use, outpatient visits, diagnostic services, emergency care, inpatient admissions and preventive services during the preceding six months. The analysis used survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression, with potential confounders identified through a directed acyclic graph. The authors also assessed robustness using Firth’s penalized regression, inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting and sensitivity analyses.

After adjustment, insurance enrollment was associated with higher odds of overall healthcare utilization (adjusted odds ratio, aOR, 2.69; 95% confidence interval, 1.56–4.63). The abstract also reports associations with outpatient use (aOR 2.13), diagnostic services (aOR 2.57), emergency care (aOR 2.81) and hospital admission (aOR 2.21), and says these findings were consistent across the sensitivity analyses. Preventive service use did not differ significantly between insured and uninsured households in the unadjusted comparison (p=0.617), and enrollment was not associated with preventive use overall (aOR 1.37). That association varied by socioeconomic status: it was positive among wealthier households (aOR 3.40) but absent among poorer households (aOR 0.40).

title: ACF to aid Nepal flood victims - Asian Hospitality
description: ACF to aid Nepal flood victims  Asian Hospitality
publisher.title: Asian Hospitality
full_article:
AS NEPAL CONTINUES to recover from a massive flood in August, U.S. hoteliers are gathering aid to send to the country. The AAHOA Charitable Foundation is organizing the effort to raise funds, donations and volunteers to bring to Nepal in January.

The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a rock-and-ice avalanche into a Himalayan mountain lake, has so far killed more than 1,400 people with more than 6000 unaccounted for, according to Big News Network. It has left more than 70,000 people homeless.

“It's so sad to see that these lives are just completely washed away, and they had no idea this was happening,” said Lina Patel, director of strategic franchise initiatives for Red Roof and one of the organizers of the ACF efforts. “We took a helicopter there to do a prayer and a puja after three weeks and you cannot tell that there was a civilization there. That whole area is back to its natural state. You cannot even see a pipe or a wire sticking out or anything. Everybody is just buried hundreds of feet under that sand and rock.”

Planning the mission

Patel regularly leads expeditions and pilgrimages in the Himalayas. She is very familiar with the area where the worst of the flood hit.

“That whole valley where villages were, that was the road that connects Nepal to China, and there was a trade route along with the Pilgrims' route, and all these villages thrive based on the trade route and the pilgrims' route,” she said. “Now that route is completely washed away, I believe the government is still deciding on what to do next.”

Fellow AAHOA lifetime members Nayna Patel, Maya Patel and Manisha Patel are serving with Lina as liaisons between ACF and Child Environment Nepal to coordinate delivery of the aid. The women, all of whom have traveled with Lina to Nepal previously, will cover their own travel expenses to visit affected communities, communicate local needs and share updates on approved relief efforts, according to ACF.

Along with cash donations, ACF are collecting staple foods, blankets and essential supplies ahead of winter. It will help fund approved recovery projects, including rebuilding homes and schools, when they go to Nepal in January. They also are looking for volunteers to join them, Lina said.

“Our plan is to go to Nepal sometimes in January to oversee the effort and do a volunteer trip,” Lina said. “We're going to invite whoever would like to come to help us do volunteer there. That way, 100 percent of the funds that are collected goes directly towards the efforts of rebuilding the lives of the families that have lost their members.”

Lina said ACF also reached out to many of the organizations across the country, such as Hindu temples and Leuva Patidar Samaj of USA. They now are collaborating with ACF.

Second mission of mercy

All four women also gathered donations for the construction of a new school in a village hit by a 2015 earthquake that also devastated Nepal. They travelled four times to oversee the project between 2015 and 2018.

“Luckily that school, which is located in this district where the flood happened, it was untouched and it's safe because it was at a much higher ground,” Patel said.

However, the flood completely wiped out a 7-story hotel where Lina and her groups would stay. Moreover, eight members of her team were killed.

“These are experienced climbers, the Sherpas,” Lina said. “There was no time for them to even go above ground.”

In 2025, members of AAHOA gathered aid for victims of the Los Angeles wildfires.

Individuals and organizations interested in supporting the ACF Nepal Relief & Recovery Fund can contribute at https://donorbox.org/acf-nepal-relief-recovery-fund.

title: Anticipating the Robert Powell Painting Retrospective - Nepali Times
description: Anticipating the Robert Powell Painting Retrospective  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Australian artist Robert Powell left a prodigious body of work across Asia that spanned Swat Valley to Angkor Wat, but it is the paintings he made while living in Nepal over 30 years that stand out.

An architect by training, the paintings show meticulous draughtsmanship and careful rendering of the colour, texture and form of Nepal’s living spaces. Powell is said to have counted every brick on the façade of the Kutu Math in Bhaktapur, or the stones in the foundations of Lo Manthang chortens before painting them.

The paintings have an almost photographic accuracy, which is why it is surprising to learn that most of his paintings were not done in situ, but back in the studio based on pencil sketches, photographs and notes he took of the site.

Powell’s prints were sold in limited edition, and many of the originals are with collectors all over the world. Now, Sophia L Pandé of The Kalā Salon in Kathmandu is curating a retrospective in 2027.

Originally planned for the Kathmandu Triennale in 2020, which had to be postponed because of Covid and Powell’s passing, the much-delayed exhibition will celebrate a talented artist who passionately loved Nepal.

But Powell rarely painted people, focusing instead on structures people built to understand them better. In that sense, his paintings represent a visual melding of architecture and anthropology. They tell stories of traditional buildings and landscapes weathered by rain, wind and time, documenting with even greater accuracy and depth than photographs.

TESTIMONIALS

Ahead of the retrospective, Pandé has come out with Robert Powell Catalogue, 2026, Verisimilitude & Imagination: A Lifetime of Paintings and Drawings. Calling it a catalogue is perhaps an understatement, since the harcover book is a collection of tributes by people who knew Powell well (Niels Gutschow, Niranjan Kunwar, Sangeeta Thapa, Lisa Choegyal, and his wife Lieve Aerts) as well as a ‘magnum opus’ by artist-architect Ross Feller.

Feller spent a week in Koh Samui in Powell’s studio just before he died in 2020, and later had access to dozens of his spiral bound sketchbooks covering 40 years. Feller analyses the pencil sketches, side notes to self, and delves deep into Powell’s mind, peeling away the artist’s technique, style, thought process and even philosophy.

Besides the artistic realism in most of his paintings, Powell also produced imaginary images of built spaces, landscapes, vegetation and terrain. As Pandé writes in the catalogue, he took ‘aspects and designs, objects and patterns and outlines of things he had seen that fascinated him, recording them in his journals and then painstakingly reworking them into iterations that are surreal and dreamlike, sometimes floating in space’.

Pandé argues that Powell’s works represent authenticity, not orientalism because ‘he does not burnish or ornament, he documents what he observes’. They can be painted goats, details of the wall at Pashupati (left), bicycles stacked with red radish, a brick kiln in Bhaktapur, or the blood-red cliffs of Drakmar.

There are even paintings of paintings, like the room in Kutu Math which was part of a series commissioned by his Austrian architect friend Götz Hagmüller who lived in that 280-year-old restored courtyard in Bhaktapur.

The Robert Powell Painting Retrospective promises to be a landmark event, the most important since his Earth Door, Sky Door, Paintings of Mustang show in 1999 at the Sackler Gallery of the Smithsonian in Washington DC.

Edited by Sophis L Pande

title: Himalayan yak herders from Bhutan, India and Nepal unite amid climate and pasture pressures - Down To Earth
description: Himalayan yak herders from Bhutan, India and Nepal unite amid climate and pasture pressures  Down To Earth
publisher.title: Down To Earth
full_article:
Yak herders from Bhutan, India and Nepal are coming together to establish the first regional network dedicated to Himalayan yak-herding communities, creating a platform for cross-border cooperation to address challenges threatening their livelihoods and traditional pastoral systems.

The Himalayan Yak Herders’ Network will be launched on October 23, 2026 at Bhutan's ninth Royal Highland Festival, as communities grapple with shrinking pastures, declining yak populations, climate change and the migration of young people from highland areas.

The network will facilitate collective advocacy, knowledge exchange, capacity building and cooperation among herders, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental organisation.

The launch follows nearly a decade of collaboration among herders, governments, researchers and development partners.

The network will bring together three national organisations — the Yak Federation of India, the Bhutan Yak Federation and the Yak and Chauri Farmers Federation Nepal. It will be led by yak herders, with Bhutan hosting its secretariat.

The idea of a regional network first emerged in 2016, when herders, researchers and government representatives from Bhutan, India and Nepal came together through ICIMOD's Kangchenjunga Landscape Conservation and Development Initiative.

Regional cooperation is particularly important because rangelands cover more than 60% of the Hindu Kush Himalaya and provide livelihoods and subsistence resources for an estimated 25–30 million Indigenous and culturally diverse people, according to the network's organisers.

Yak-herding communities face growing pressures from rangeland degradation, loss of yak genetic diversity, attacks on livestock by wild animals and limited access to markets and essential services. These challenges are compounded by climate change and the migration of younger generations away from highland areas.

According to ICIMOD, yak populations across Bhutan, India and Nepal have declined significantly in recent decades, partly because of changing land-use patterns and rangeland degradation.

In India, the 20th Livestock Census, published in 2019, recorded approximately 58,000 yaks.

In 2026, the Yak Federation of India reported that 526 household members associated with the federation collectively reared approximately 32,000 yaks.

title: Ireland Drawn With India, West Indies and Nepal for U19 Women’s T20 World Cup - Sport for Business
description: Ireland Drawn With India, West Indies and Nepal for U19 Women’s T20 World Cup  Sport for Business
publisher.title: Sport for Business
full_article:
Ireland will face defending champions India, the West Indies and co-hosts Nepal in the group stages of the ICC U19 Women’s T20 World Cup in January and February 2027.

The International Cricket Council’s schedule places Ireland in Group A for the third edition of a tournament that is an increasingly important part of the pathway for emerging female cricketers.

When the tournament was last held in 2025, Ireland scored a huge win by advancing to the Super Six stage.

This latest generation will open its campaign against Nepal in Kathmandu on January 22, while India will begin its bid for a third successive title against the West Indies later that day at TU International Cricket Stadium.

Sixteen countries will compete across 41 matches in Bangladesh and Nepal between January 21 and February 6.

For Cricket Ireland, qualification and participation offer another significant international opportunity for players at an age when the transition from underage to senior cricket can be critical.

The ICC has established the competition as an elite development platform and a world championship in its own right, giving young players experience of international tournament structures, travel, and preparation against leading cricket nations.

That makes a group containing India particularly valuable from an Irish perspective. India have won both previous editions of the competition and are already a dominant force in the global development of the women’s game.

The West Indies offer another established cricketing test, while the opening fixture against Nepal will add the challenge of facing one of the host nations in Kathmandu.

The initial group stage runs until January 26, after which the leading teams advance to the Super Six stage. The remaining nations will then compete for places in the semi-finals, scheduled for February 4.

The final will take place on February 6, with February 7 retained as a reserve day.

Matches will be played across four venues: the Bir Shrestha Shahid Flight Lieutenant Matiur Rahman Cricket Stadium in Chattogram, Sylhet International Cricket Stadium, TU International Cricket Stadium in Kathmandu and Upper Mulpani International Cricket Ground.

Sport for Business Perspective

Women’s cricket has been one of the clearest growth opportunities available to the sport internationally, and the strength of any national programme increasingly depends on whether there is a credible pathway beneath senior level.

An Under-19 World Cup provides exactly that.

It offers players meaningful competition against countries operating at very different levels of scale, resources and playing population. It also gives coaches and high-performance staff an important benchmark for where Ireland sits internationally as players approach senior cricket.

Major international tournaments create stories and identifiable players at an age when younger participants at home can still see a relatively short distance between their own club or school cricket and representing Ireland.

That connection between participation, pathway, and international opportunity is important if Irish cricket is to keep broadening the base of the women’s game.

Facing India, the West Indies and Nepal will make progression challenging, but it is precisely the type of competitive environment Ireland needs its best young players to experience.

Thailand’s and Nepal’s Oscar submissions, “9 Temples to Heaven” and “Elephants in the Fog,” are among 10 titles competing at the 27th edition of Tokyo Filmex, which will run Nov. 20–29 in the Japanese capital’s Yurakucho district.

The panel will pick a Grand Prize winner, whose director will receive JPY700,000 ($4,500), and a Special Jury Prize winner, whose director will receive JPY300,000 ($1,900). ICIMOD satellite analysis detected instability nearly seven weeks before Aug 26 disaster; SMS warnings reached residents after debris flood swept through border corridor. (AFP)

A Himalayan mountain slope had shifted by up to 40cm over 48 days before it collapsed, triggering the devastating Aug 26 flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, a scientific assessment released on Tuesday by International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found. The disaster killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal and left 5,745 missing, while another 43 died and 519 remained missing in China. The findings indicated that satellite monitoring could detect unstable slopes weeks before collapse, though scientists said predicting the precise timing remained difficult.The preliminary report, Understanding the Gyirong-Rasuwa Disaster of 26 August 2026, analysed Sentinel-1 satellite radar observations from July 7 to Aug 24 and recorded ground movement of up to 40cm along the satellite’s line of sight. The deformation pointed to growing instability in the rock and ice mass before its collapse.At 8.37am on Aug 26, an estimated 132 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice broke away from the northern face of Langtang Lirung and plunged into Lhende Khola valley, sending a torrent of debris downstream. The surge reached the border corridor in approximately seven minutes, but authorities issued SMS warnings only around 9.15–9.16am — nearly 38–39 minutes after the collapse and about half an hour after the flood reached the corridor.The assessment drew on satellite imagery, seismic records, drone surveys, hydrological analysis and field investigations. Researchers identified geological weaknesses, possible damage from the 2015 Nepal earthquake, thawing permafrost, glacier changes and snow accumulation as potential contributing factors, but could not establish a single trigger.The study ruled out a conventional glacial lake outburst flood, initially suspected as the cause. Instead, a massive bedrock failure dislodged part of an overlying glacier, triggering a cascading flow of rock, ice, water and sediment through the valley.Researchers said conventional early-warning systems focused on rainfall and river levels were inadequate for detecting sudden mountain collapses capable of generating fast-moving debris floods.“This tragedy shows that some dangerous mountain slopes may exhibit measurable signs of instability before catastrophic failure,” said ICIMOD director general Pema Gyamtsho.ICIMOD scientist Qianggong Zhang said satellite-based monitoring could help identify other potentially unstable slopes for closer observation, although researchers could not reliably determine when they might collapse.The findings came two days after another major rock-ice avalanche and flood struck Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki basin on Oct 11, raising concerns about the monitoring of unstable slopes across the Himalayas.A joint scientific field investigation involving ICIMOD and Chinese researchers was scheduled to begin this week to examine the disaster site and identify other potential hazard hotspots across the Himalayan region.
